title: Daily routine, telling the time and reflexive verbs
objectives: I can describe a typical day with verbs such as 'прокида́тися', 'встава́ти', 'сні́дати', 'обі́дати' and 'вече́ряти'.
I can form the present of a reflexive verb, choose between '-ся' and '-сь', and say '-ться' and '-шся' correctly.
I can ask 'Котра́ годи́на?' and 'О котрі́й?' and answer with an ordinal numeral, including half hours with 'пів на'.
I can say when something happens with 'вра́нці', 'уве́чері' and 'вночі́'.
I can say how often I do something, and use 'ніко́ли' with 'не' before the verb.

vocabulary.note: The present is 'прокида́юся' or 'прокида́юсь', 'прокида́єшся', 'прокида́ється'. Here '-ся' adds no idea of 'oneself': it only marks that the verb has no object.
The present is 'встаю́', 'встає́ш', 'встаю́ть': the '-ва-' of the infinitive drops in the present. It means getting out of bed, which comes after 'прокида́тися', and it has no '-ся'.
It is regular like 'чита́ти', with '-ся' added: 'одяга́юся', 'одяга́єшся'. Without '-ся', the verb 'одяга́ти' means to dress someone else.
It is one verb where English uses 'have' and a noun. It is regular like 'чита́ти': 'сні́даю', 'сні́даєш'.

example.source: Do you have breakfast in the kitchen?

vocabulary.note: It is built on the noun 'обі́д', the main meal of the middle of the day. It is regular: 'обі́даю', 'обі́даєш'.
It is built on the noun 'вече́ря', the evening meal, which is related to 'ве́чір'. It is regular: 'вече́ряю', 'вече́ряєш'.

example.source: They have dinner at the café.

vocabulary.note: It is second conjugation although it ends in '-ати': 'сплю', 'спиш', 'спить', 'спимо́', 'спите́', 'сплять'. After 'п' the forms for 'я' and 'вони́' add 'л', as 'люблю́' does.
In clock times it is the noun the ordinal numeral agrees with, and it is usually left out: 'Сьо́ма.' is short for 'Сьо́ма годи́на.'
After the numbers that take 'ро́ків', such as 'п’ять' and 'де́сять', it takes the form 'хвили́н', met whole like 'ро́ків'.

example.source: It is ten past six now.

vocabulary.note: 'Пів' is a numeral that names half of something. It never changes, and with 'на' and the accusative of the next hour it gives the half hour: 'пів на восьму́', 7:30, literally 'half on eighth'.

example.target: Я обі́даю о пів на дру́гу.
example.source: I have lunch at half past one.
example.source_literal: I have-lunch at half on second.

vocabulary.note: The other forms are 'котра́', 'котре́', 'котрі́'. It asks for a place in an order, so the answer is an ordinal numeral. In clock times it is feminine, agreeing with 'годи́на'.
The genitive is 'но́чі'. It is a feminine noun in a consonant, like 'сіль'. The 'і' of the closed syllable becomes 'о' when an ending opens it.

example.source: He works until late at night.

vocabulary.note: It is built from 'в' and the root of 'ра́нок'. Its first letter follows the euphony of 'у' and 'в': after a consonant and at the start of a sentence it is 'ура́нці'.

example.source: I drink coffee in the morning.

vocabulary.note: It is built from 'у' and 'ве́чір', whose 'і' becomes 'е' in this form. It always begins with 'у', because the euphony rule puts 'у' before 'в'.
It is built from 'в' and 'ніч'. After a consonant and at the start of a sentence it is 'уночі́'.

example.source: The city is very beautiful at night.

vocabulary.note: It grew from a phrase meaning 'by custom'.

example.source: I usually have breakfast at home.
We often have lunch at the café.

vocabulary.note: The verb after it takes 'не' as well: 'ніко́ли не сні́даю', literally 'never not I-have-breakfast'.

dialogues.title: Two weekday mornings
dialogues.context: Sam and Oksana meet at Andrii's café early on a weekday morning, before their day begins. They are friends and use 'ти'.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.source: Hi, Sam! How are you?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре, дя́кую. Але́ я хо́чу спа́ти.
lines.source: Fine, thanks. But I want to sleep.
lines.source_literal: Well, I-thank. But I want to-sleep.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.source: What time do you wake up?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.source: Usually at six. And you?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А я прокида́юся о восьмі́й і шви́дко одяга́юся.
lines.source: I wake up at eight and get dressed quickly.
lines.source_literal: And I wake-up at eighth and quickly dress-self.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.source: And do you have breakfast?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ні, я ніко́ли не сні́даю. Тут я п’ю ка́ву.
lines.source: No, I never have breakfast. I drink coffee here.
lines.source_literal: No, I never not have-breakfast. Here I drink coffee.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А я завжди́ сні́даю вдо́ма. Я їм хліб і сир.
lines.source: I always have breakfast at home. I eat bread and cheese.
lines.source_literal: And I always have-breakfast at-home. I eat bread and cheese.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.source: And what time is it now?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.source: Twenty past eight.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Я ї́ду на метро́ о пів на дев’я́ту. Бува́й, Се́ме!
lines.source: I take the metro at half past eight. Bye, Sam!
lines.source_literal: I ride on metro at half on ninth. Bye, Sam!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.source: Bye, Oksana!

dialogues.title: Sam's day
dialogues.context: Before class, Iryna Petrivna asks Sam about his day. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.source: Good morning, Sam!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.source: Good morning, Iryna Petrivna!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Се́ме, о котрі́й ви зазвича́й прокида́єтеся?
lines.source: Sam, what time do you usually wake up?
lines.source_literal: Sam, at which you usually wake-up?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: О шо́стій ра́нку, а встаю́ о сьо́мій.
lines.source: At six in the morning, but I get up at seven.
lines.source_literal: At sixth of-morning, and I-get-up at seventh.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.source: And what do you do in the morning?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я одяга́юся, сні́даю й п’ю ка́ву.
lines.source: I get dressed, have breakfast and drink coffee.
lines.source_literal: I dress-self, have-breakfast and drink coffee.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А о котрі́й ви йдете́ в університе́т?
lines.source: And what time do you go to the university?
lines.source_literal: And at which you go to university?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: О пів на дев’я́ту. Університе́т бли́зько.
lines.source: At half past eight. The university is close by.
lines.source_literal: At half on ninth. University close.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.source: And in the evening, do you read in Ukrainian?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, і́ноді. Але́ вночі́ я сплю!
lines.source: Yes, sometimes. But at night I sleep!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.source: What time do you go to bed?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.source: Usually at eleven.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.source: That's good. Goodbye, Sam!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.source: Goodbye!

dialogues.title: When is lunch?
dialogues.context: Taras and his colleague Sofiia are at work in the late morning. They are colleagues of the same age and use 'ти'.

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.source: Taras, what time is it?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.source: It's five past eleven.

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.source: Are we having lunch at one today?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ні, сього́дні о пів на дру́гу.
lines.source: No, today at half past one.
lines.source_literal: No, today at half on second.

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.source: And why not at one?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Тому́ що сього́дні я працю́ю ду́же пові́льно.
lines.source: Because today I'm working very slowly.

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.target: Ти ча́сто обі́даєш тут, на робо́ті?
lines.source: Do you often have lunch here at work?
lines.source_literal: You often have-lunch here, on work?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ні, і́ноді. Зазвича́й я обі́даю в кафе́ бі́ля па́рку.
lines.source: No, only sometimes. I usually have lunch at the café near the park.
lines.source_literal: No, sometimes. Usually I have-lunch in café near park.

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.target: А я ніко́ли не обі́даю в кафе́.
lines.source: And I never have lunch at a café.
lines.source_literal: And I never not have-lunch in café.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.source: Never? Then where do you have lunch?

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.target: Тут. Я завжди́ їм суп моє́ї ма́ми.
lines.source: Here. I always eat my mom's soup.
lines.source_literal: Here. I always eat soup of-my of-mom.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: До́бре, обі́даємо тут о пів на дру́гу.
lines.source: All right, we'll have lunch here at half past one.
lines.source_literal: Well, we-have-lunch here at half on second.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: '-ться', '-шся' and the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Every new word of this unit can be read with the rules of the first four units, apart from two endings of reflexive verbs. In them two consonant letters meet and merge into one long soft consonant, so they are not said letter by letter. A long consonant is held a little longer than a short one, as in 'життя́' (unit 3), but here no letter is doubled.

- '-ться' ends the forms for 'він' and 'вони́' and is said [t͡sʲːɑ]: the soft 'т' and the 'с' merge into a long soft 'ц'. 'Прокида́ється' is [prɔkɪˈdɑjɛt͡sʲːɑ], and 'одяга́ються' is [ɔdʲɑˈɦɑjut͡sʲːɑ].
- '-шся' ends the form for 'ти' and is said [sʲːɑ]: the 'ш' takes on the softness of the 'с' after it and merges with it into a long soft 'с'. 'Прокида́єшся' is [prɔkɪˈdɑjɛsʲːɑ].
- '-ся' after a vowel is said as it is written, a soft 'с' and [ɑ]: 'прокида́юся' is [prɔkɪˈdɑjusʲɑ]. The short form '-сь' is a soft 'с' alone: 'прокида́юсь' is [prɔkɪˈdɑjusʲ].

The same long [t͡sʲː] is the 'дц' of 'одина́дцять' (unit 11), so 'одина́дцята' and 'двана́дцята' are read in the same way.

The other new words apply familiar rules:

- 'Сні́дати': 'н' is soft before 'і', and 'д' is hard before 'а'.
- 'Сьо́ма' and 'восьма́': 'ьо' writes a soft consonant followed by [ɔ] (unit 3), so 'сьо' is [sʲɔ].
- 'Тре́тя' and 'вече́ряти': a consonant before 'я' is soft, 'т' in the first word and 'р' in the second.
- 'П’я́та' and 'дев’я́та': the apostrophe keeps 'п' and 'в' hard and the [j] of 'я' sounded (unit 3).
- 'Вра́нці', 'вночі́', 'встава́ти' and 'завжди́': 'в' before a consonant is [w], as at the end of 'Львів'.
- 'Сім' and 'сьо́ма', 'шість' and 'шо́ста', 'ніч' and 'но́чі', 'ве́чір' and 'ве́чора': the 'і' of a closed syllable becomes 'о' when an ending opens the syllable, the alternation of 'кіт' and 'кота́' (unit 5).
- 'Ві́сім' gives 'восьма́', stressed on the ending: the first 'і' becomes 'о', and the second disappears, leaving a soft 'с' marked by 'ь'.
- 'Де́в’ять' and 'де́сять' move the stress to the second syllable in their ordinals: 'дев’я́та', 'деся́та'. 'Чоти́ри' gives 'четве́рта', on a changed stem that is learned as it is.
- 'Ра́нок' gives 'ра́нку', and 'день' gives 'дня': the 'о' or 'е' of the last syllable drops when an ending is added.
- 'Встава́ти' drops '-ва-' in the present: 'встаю́', 'встає́ш', where 'ю' and 'є' after a vowel are [ju] and [jɛ].
- 'Спа́ти' adds 'л' after 'п' in 'сплю' and 'сплять', as 'люби́ти' does in 'люблю́' (unit 9), and its stress moves to the ending in 'спимо́' and 'спите́'.

rows: 'і' in a closed syllable, 'о' in an open one

examples.source: Do you wake up at eight?

grammar.title: Reflexive verbs: the suffix '-ся'
grammar.explanation:
A reflexive verb is a verb with the suffix '-ся' at its very end, after the infinitive ending or the personal ending. A suffix is a part added at the end of a word, and '-ся' is always written joined to the verb. It goes back to an old short word meaning 'oneself', but today it is part of the verb: not a separate word, and not a pronoun. A dictionary gives a reflexive verb with '-ся' in the infinitive: 'прокида́тися', 'одяга́тися'.

The suffix does one of two jobs:

- The action returns to the subject, which does it to itself. 'Одяга́ти' is to dress someone: 'Ма́ма одяга́є дити́ну.', 'Mom dresses the child.' 'Одяга́тися' is to dress oneself, to get dressed: 'Дити́на одяга́ється.'
- The verb simply has no object, with no idea of 'oneself'. 'Прокида́тися' means 'to wake up', and nothing returns to the subject: here '-ся' only marks that the verb has no object.

Whether a verb takes '-ся' is learned with the verb, because English gives no sign of it: 'to wake up' is 'прокида́тися', but 'to get up' is 'встава́ти', with no '-ся'.

To form the present, conjugate the verb as if '-ся' were not there, then add the suffix. 'Прокида́тися' and 'одяга́тися' conjugate like 'чита́ти', and only two things change:

- In the form for 'він', 'вона́' and 'воно́', 'ть' appears before the suffix: 'одяга́є' becomes 'одяга́ється'. This 'ть' is an old personal ending that the plain form has dropped and the reflexive form keeps.
- After a vowel the suffix can be '-ся' or the shorter '-сь', and both are standard: 'прокида́юся' or 'прокида́юсь', 'прокида́ємося' or 'прокида́ємось', and in the infinitive 'прокида́тися' or 'прокида́тись'. After a consonant it is always '-ся': 'прокида́єшся', 'прокида́ється', 'прокида́ються'.

The full present of 'прокида́тися':

- я прокида́юся
- ти прокида́єшся
- він, вона́, воно́ прокида́ється
- ми прокида́ємося
- ви прокида́єтеся
- вони́ прокида́ються

The suffix always comes last, so 'не' and every other word stay outside the verb: 'Я не прокида́юся вночі́.'

examples.source: I do not wake up at night.

grammar.title: Telling the time: 'Котра́ годи́на?' and 'О котрі́й?'
grammar.explanation:
English tells the time with cardinal numbers: 'one o'clock', 'seven o'clock'. Ukrainian counts the hours of the day as places in an order, the way English counts floors or birthdays, so it uses ordinal numerals: 'сьо́ма годи́на', literally 'seventh hour', is seven o'clock. An ordinal numeral names a place in an order: first, second, third. Ukrainian ordinals are numerals, but they take the endings of adjectives and agree with their noun in gender, number and case. Most are built on the stem of the cardinal numeral (unit 11) with an adjective ending: 'п’ять', 'п’я́та'; 'де́сять', 'деся́та'. 'Пе́рша' and 'дру́га' come from other roots than 'оди́н' and 'два'. 'Тре́тя' has a soft stem, like 'си́ня' (unit 8), so it has '-я' and '-ю' where the others have '-а' and '-у'. In clock times they are feminine, because they agree with 'годи́на', which is feminine, and 'годи́на' itself is usually left out.

The question uses 'котри́й', which asks for a place in an order, also in the feminine: 'Котра́ годи́на?', literally 'which hour?', means 'What time is it?'. The answer is the ordinal alone or with 'годи́на', often with 'за́раз', now: 'Сьо́ма.', 'За́раз сьо́ма годи́на.'

To say at what time something happens, put 'о' before the ordinal in the locative: 'о сьо́мій', literally 'at seventh', is at seven. 'О' is a preposition that takes the locative and means 'at' with clock times, and the ordinal takes the feminine locative ending '-ій' that adjectives take ('у вели́кій кімна́ті', unit 12). The question is 'О котрі́й?', 'At what time?'. Before a vowel 'о' becomes 'об', so that two vowels do not meet: 'об одина́дцятій'. The table gives each hour in the three forms that clock times use most: the nominative for the time it is, the locative after 'о', and the accusative after 'на'.

Between the full hours, Ukrainian counts toward the next hour, because the time after seven o'clock is already part of the eighth hour:

- 'Пів на восьму́', literally 'half on eighth', is 7:30. 'Пів' means 'half' and never changes, and 'на' takes the accusative of the hour under way, with the feminine ending '-у' or '-ю' of unit 10: 'восьму́', 'тре́тю'.
- With 'пів', 'о' stands before the whole phrase: 'о пів на восьму́', at 7:30.
- 'П’ять хвили́н на восьму́', literally 'five of-minutes on eighth', is 7:05, and 'де́сять хвили́н на восьму́' is 7:10. 'Хвили́н' is the form of 'хвили́на' after the numbers that take 'ро́ків' (unit 11), met whole like 'ро́ків'. Where unit 11 has 'рік', the noun is 'хвили́на', and where it has 'ро́ки', it is 'хвили́ни': 'одна́ хвили́на', 'дві хвили́ни'.
- After the half hour, the simplest way is the ordinal followed by the minutes as a cardinal number: 'сьо́ма со́рок', 7:40.
- 'До' with the genitive gives 'until': 'до восьмо́ї', until eight, with the feminine genitive ending '-ої' (unit 14).

To show which half of the day is meant, add the genitive of a part of the day after the time: 'о сьо́мій ра́нку', at seven in the morning, literally 'at seventh of-morning'; 'о дев’я́тій ве́чора', at nine in the evening; 'о дру́гій но́чі', literally 'at second of-night', at two in the morning. Ukrainian counts the first hours after midnight as night, where English already says 'in the morning'. 'Ра́нку' is the genitive of 'ра́нок', the morning of 'до́брий ра́нок'; 'ве́чора' is the genitive of 'ве́чір', and 'но́чі' the genitive of 'ніч'.

examples.source: What time is it? Two o'clock.
What time do you have lunch?

examples.target: Сем іде́ в університе́т о пів на дев’я́ту.
examples.source: Sam goes to the university at half past eight.
examples.source_literal: Sam goes to university at half on ninth.

examples.source: We have dinner at seven in the evening.

grammar.title: Parts of the day and how often: 'вра́нці', 'ча́сто', 'ніко́ли не'
grammar.explanation:
English says when something happens with a preposition and a noun: 'in the morning', 'at night'. Ukrainian uses one word, an adverb that grew out of a preposition joined to an old case form of a noun:

- 'вра́нці', in the morning, from 'в' and the root of 'ра́нок'
- 'уве́чері', in the evening, from 'у' and 'ве́чір'
- 'вночі́', at night, from 'в' and 'ніч'

They are adverbs, so they take no case endings, and they usually stand before the verb: 'Вона́ вра́нці п’є чай.' Their first letter is still the old preposition and follows the euphony rule of unit 4: after a consonant and at the start of a sentence they are written and said 'ура́нці' and 'уночі́', as in 'Сем уночі́ чита́є.' 'Уве́чері' always has 'у', because 'у' stands before 'в'. With a clock time, use the genitive of the noun instead: 'о сьо́мій ра́нку' (previous note).

Frequency adverbs say how often something happens. From most often to least often:

- 'завжди́', always
- 'зазвича́й', usually
- 'ча́сто', often
- 'і́ноді', sometimes
- 'ніко́ли', never

Like 'до́бре' and 'шви́дко' (unit 9), they usually come right before the verb: 'Я ча́сто чита́ю.' They can also open the sentence, which sets the frame for what follows: 'Зазвича́й я обі́даю тут.'

'Ніко́ли' follows a rule that English does not have. A Ukrainian negative word such as 'ніко́ли' does not make a sentence negative on its own: the verb takes 'не' as well. 'Я ніко́ли не сні́даю.' is literally 'I never not have-breakfast'. In English two negatives cancel each other out; in Ukrainian they reinforce each other, and the sentence means 'I never have breakfast'. This is called a double negative. Alone, as a short answer, 'ніко́ли' needs no verb and no 'не': 'Ти ча́сто обі́даєш тут?' 'Ніко́ли.'

'Не' before 'завжди́' or 'ча́сто' simply negates the adverb: 'Я не завжди́ сні́даю.', 'I do not always have breakfast.'

rows: Part of the day before the verb
She drinks tea in the morning.
We sometimes have lunch at home.
I never have dinner at night.

examples.target: Окса́на зазвича́й ї́де в університе́т на метро́.
examples.source: Oksana usually takes the metro to the university.
examples.source_literal: Oksana usually rides to university on metro.

examples.source: Do you often read in the evening?
I do not always have breakfast.

culture.title: The working day and the clock in Ukraine
culture.text:
Ukrainian schools usually begin the first lesson at eight or half past eight, and many offices open at nine. Traditionally the main meal of the day is 'обі́д', eaten at midday or early in the afternoon, and it often begins with a soup such as borscht. The soup course is called 'пе́рше', the first, and the main course 'дру́ге', the second: these are the neuter forms of the ordinal numerals 'пе́рший' and 'дру́гий', used on their own as nouns. The evening meal is 'вече́ря', the noun behind the verb 'вече́ряти'.

Timetables, tickets and official notices use the twenty-four-hour clock, read with the same ordinal numerals. In a compound ordinal only the last word is an ordinal: 'два́дцять пе́рша', 21:00, is literally 'twenty first'. In conversation people usually keep to the twelve-hour clock and add the part of the day in the genitive:

- 'о сьо́мій ра́нку', at seven in the morning
- 'о тре́тій дня', at three in the afternoon
- 'о дев’я́тій ве́чора', at nine in the evening
- 'о дру́гій но́чі', at two in the morning

'Дня' is the genitive of 'день', which loses its 'е' in its other forms.

When Ukrainians name a time between two hours, they think of the hour that has begun rather than the one that has passed: at 7:30 the eighth hour is half over, so the time is 'пів на восьму́'. Listen for this when someone arranges to meet you: 'пів на восьму́' is half past seven, not half past eight.

exercises.explanation: 'Котри́й' asks for a place in an order, and Ukrainian counts the hours in order, so 'Котра́ годи́на?', literally 'which hour?', asks the time. 'At what time?' is 'О котрі́й?'.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian with the English

exercises.explanation: A reflexive verb carries the suffix '-ся'. 'Прокида́тися' has it; 'встава́ти', 'to get up', does not. Whether a verb takes '-ся' is learned with the verb.
Ukrainian counts toward the hour under way: at 7:30 the eighth hour is half over, so the time is 'half on eighth'.

choices: They often have lunch at the café.
They sometimes have lunch at the café.
They sometimes have breakfast at the café.

exercises.explanation: 'Одяга́ти', without '-ся', takes an object: the person being dressed, here 'дити́ну' in the accusative. 'Mom gets dressed' would be 'Ма́ма одяга́ється.'
The form for 'я' is 'прокида́ю' plus the suffix. After a vowel the suffix can be '-ся' or '-сь', so both forms are correct.
'At' a clock time is 'о' with the locative, '-ій'. Before a vowel 'о' becomes 'об'. 'Одина́дцята' says that it is eleven o'clock, and 'о деся́тій' is at ten.
In the form for 'він', 'ть' appears before the suffix: 'одяга́є' becomes 'одяга́ється'. After 'ть' only '-ся' is possible.
The hour is an ordinal numeral, feminine to agree with 'годи́на': 'четве́рта', the fourth.
After 'о' the ordinal takes the feminine locative ending '-ій': 'о дру́гій', literally 'at second'.

exercises.explanation: With 'ніко́ли' the verb also takes 'не'. The two negatives reinforce each other, and the sentence means 'never'.

It agrees with 'хвили́на', which is left out.
Clock times are adverbs, and these adverbs end in '-а'.
exercises.explanation: 'Сьо́ма' is an ordinal numeral, and ordinals agree like adjectives. 'Сьо́ма' is short for 'сьо́ма годи́на', the seventh hour.

exercises.prompt: Which form can also end in '-сь'?
exercises.explanation: '-сь' replaces '-ся' only after a vowel: 'прокида́ємо' ends in 'о', so 'прокида́ємось' is also correct. The other forms have '-ся' after a consonant, 'ть' or 'ш'.

exercises.prompt_target: Оле́на ї́де на робо́ту о пів на ___.
exercises.hint_source: Olena goes to work at half past seven.
exercises.explanation: Half past seven is half of the eighth hour, so 'на' takes the accusative of the ordinal for eight: 'восьму́'.

exercises.prompt: What time is 'п’ять хвили́н на восьму́'?
exercises.explanation: The minutes count into the hour under way: five minutes into the eighth hour is 7:05.
'Встава́ти' drops '-ва-' in the present, so the form for 'я' is 'встаю́'. 'At seven' is 'о сьо́мій'.

exercises.prompt: In 'Я ніко́ли не сні́даю.', what does 'не' do?

It is required with 'ніко́ли', and the sentence means 'I never have breakfast'.
It turns the sentence into a question.
exercises.explanation: A Ukrainian negative word needs 'не' before the verb as well. The two negatives reinforce each other; they do not cancel.
